Asia
Asia is the largest <color=#3366CC>continent</color> in the world by both land area and population. It covers an area of more than 44 million
square kilometres, about 30% of Earth's total land area and 8% of Earth's total surface area. The continent, which has
long been home to the majority of the human population, was the site of many of the <color=#3366CC>first civilisations</color>. Its 4.7 billion
people constitute roughly 60% of the world's population.

Asia shares the landmass of <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color> with <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>, and of <color=#3366CC>Afro-Eurasia</color> with both Europe and <color=#3366CC>Africa</color>. In general terms, it
is bounded on the east by the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean</color>, on the south by the <color=#3366CC>Indian Ocean</color>, and on the north by the <color=#3366CC>Arctic Ocean</color>.
The border of Asia with Europe is a <color=#3366CC>historical and cultural construct</color>, as there is no clear physical and geographical
separation between them. A commonly accepted division places Asia to the east of the <color=#3366CC>Suez Canal</color> separating it from
Africa; and to the east of the Turkish straits, the <color=#3366CC>Ural Mountains</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ural River</color>, and to the south of the <color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color>
<color=#3366CC>Mountains</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Caspian</color> and <color=#3366CC>Black</color> seas, separating it from Europe.
Since the concept of Asia derives from the term for the eastern region from a European perspective, Asia is the
remaining vast area of Eurasia minus Europe. Therefore, Asia is a region where various independent cultures coexist
rather than sharing a single culture, and its boundary with Europe is somewhat arbitrary and has moved since its first
conception in <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color>. The division of Eurasia into two continents reflects East–West cultural differences,
some of which vary on a spectrum.
<color=#3366CC>China</color> and <color=#3366CC>India</color> traded places as the largest economies in the world from 1 to 1800 CE. China was a major economic
power for much of recorded history, with the highest <color=#3366CC>GDP per capita</color> until 1500. The <color=#3366CC>Silk Road</color> became the main
east–west trading route in the Asian hinterlands while the <color=#3366CC>Straits of Malacca</color> stood as a major sea route. Asia has
exhibited economic dynamism as well as robust population growth during the 20th century, but overall population
growth has since fallen. Asia was the birthplace of most of the world's mainstream religions including <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, <color=#3366CC>Judaism</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>, and many other religions.
Asia varies greatly across and within <color=#3366CC>its regions</color> with regard to <color=#3366CC>ethnic groups</color>, cultures, environments, economics,
historical ties, and government systems. It also has a mix of many different climates ranging from the equatorial south

via the hot deserts in parts of <color=#3366CC>West Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color> and tropical jungles in <color=#3366CC>Southeast</color>
<color=#3366CC>Asia</color>, temperate areas in the east and the continental centre to vast subarctic and polar areas in <color=#3366CC>North Asia</color>.
Etymology
The term "Asia" is believed to originate in the <color=#3366CC>Bronze Age</color> toponym Assuwa (aš-šu-wa) which originally referred only to
a portion of northwestern <color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color>. The term appears in Hittite records recounting how a confederation of Assuwan
states including <color=#3366CC>Troy</color> unsuccessfully rebelled against the Hittite king Tudhaliya I around 1400 BCE. Roughly
contemporary <color=#3366CC>Linear B</color> documents contain the term aswia (a-si-wi-ja), seemingly in reference to captives from the same
area.
Herodotus used the term in reference to <color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color> and the territory of the <color=#3366CC>Achaemenid Empire</color>, in contrast to Greece and
Egypt. He reports that Greeks assumed that Asia was named after the wife of <color=#3366CC>Prometheus</color>, but that <color=#3366CC>Lydians</color> say it was
named after Asies, son of Cotys, who passed the name on to a tribe at Sardis. In <color=#3366CC>Greek mythology</color>, "Asia" ( or ) was the

name of a "<color=#3366CC>Nymph</color> or <color=#3366CC>Titan</color> goddess of Lydia". The <color=#3366CC>Iliad</color> (attributed by the ancient Greeks to <color=#3366CC>Homer</color>) mentions two
Phrygians in the <color=#3366CC>Trojan War</color> named Asios (literally 'Asian'); and also a marsh or lowland containing a marsh in Lydia as.
The term was later adopted by the Romans, who used it in reference to the province of Asia, located in western
Anatolia. One of the first writers to use Asia as a name of the whole continent was <color=#3366CC>Pliny</color>.
Definition
Asia–Europe boundary
The threefold division of the <color=#3366CC>Old World</color> into Africa, Asia, and Europe has been in use since the 6th century BCE, due to
Greek geographers such as <color=#3366CC>Anaximander</color> and Hecataeus. Anaximander placed the boundary between Asia and
Europe along the Phasis River (now the Rioni) in <color=#3366CC>Georgia</color> of Caucasus (from its mouth by Poti on the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color> coast,
through the Surami Pass and along the <color=#3366CC>Kura River</color> to the Caspian Sea), a convention still followed by <color=#3366CC>Herodotus</color> in the
5th century BCE. During the <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic period</color>, this convention was revised, and the boundary between Europe and
Asia was now considered to be the <color=#3366CC>Tanais</color> (the modern Don River). This is the convention used by Roman era authors
such as <color=#3366CC>Posidonius</color>, <color=#3366CC>Strabo</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ptolemy</color>.
The border between Asia and Europe was later redefined by European academics. In 1730, five years after the death
of <color=#3366CC>Peter the Great</color>, Philip Johan von Strahlenberg published in Sweden a new atlas proposing the Ural Mountains as
the border of Asia. Vasily Tatishchev announced that he had proposed the idea to von Strahlenberg. The latter had
suggested the <color=#3366CC>Emba River</color> as the southern part of this boundary. Over the next century various proposals were made
until the <color=#3366CC>Ural River</color> prevailed in the mid-19th century. The border had been moved perforce from the Black Sea (the
Romans' definition) to the Caspian Sea into which the Emba and Ural rivers project. Between the Black Sea and the
Caspian, the border is often placed along the crest of the <color=#3366CC>Caucasus Mountains</color>, although it is sometimes placed further
north, on the Kuma–Manych Depression.
Asia–Africa boundary
The boundary between Asia and Africa is the <color=#3366CC>Suez Canal</color>, the Gulf of Suez, the <color=#3366CC>Red Sea</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Bab-el-Mandeb</color>. This
makes <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color> a transcontinental country, with the <color=#3366CC>Sinai Peninsula</color> in Asia and the remainder of the country in Africa.
Asia–Oceania boundary
The border between Asia and <color=#3366CC>Oceania</color> is usually placed somewhere in the Indonesian Archipelago, specifically in
Eastern Indonesia. The Wallace Line separates the Asian and Wallacea biogeographical realms, a transition zone of
deep water straits between the Asian and Australian continental shelves. Weber's Line split the region in two with
regard to the balance of fauna between Asian origin or Australo-Papuan origin. Wallacea's eastern boundary with <color=#3366CC>Sahul</color>
is represented by the Lydekker's Line. The <color=#3366CC>Maluku Islands</color> (except the <color=#3366CC>Aru Islands</color>) are often considered to lie on the
border of southeast Asia, with the Aru Islands and <color=#3366CC>Western New Guinea</color>, to the east of the Lydekker's Line, being
wholly part of Oceania, as both lie on the Australian continental plate. Culturally, the Wallacea region denoted the
transition between <color=#3366CC>Austronesian</color> and <color=#3366CC>Melanesian people</color>, with varying degrees of intermixing between the two. In
general, the further west and coastal a region is, the stronger the Austronesian influences, and the further east and
inland a region is, the stronger the Melanesian influences. The terms Southeast Asia and Oceania, devised in the 19th
century, have had several vastly different geographic meanings since their inception. The chief factor in determining
which islands of the Indonesian Archipelago are Asian has been the location of the colonial possessions of the various
empires there (not all European). Lewis and Wigen assert, "The narrowing of 'Southeast Asia' to its present boundaries
was thus a gradual process."
Asia–North America boundary
The <color=#3366CC>Bering Strait</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bering Sea</color> separate the landmasses of Asia and <color=#3366CC>North America</color>, as well as forming the
international boundary between Russia and the United States. This <color=#3366CC>national</color> and continental boundary separates the
Diomede Islands in the Bering Strait, with Big Diomede in <color=#3366CC>Russia</color> and Little Diomede in the <color=#3366CC>United States</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Aleutian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Islands</color> are an island chain extending westward from the <color=#3366CC>Alaskan Peninsula</color> toward Russia's <color=#3366CC>Komandorski Islands</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Kamchatka Peninsula</color>. Most of them are always associated with North America, except for the westernmost Near
Islands group, which is on Asia's continental shelf beyond the North Aleutians Basin and on rare occasions could be
associated with Asia, which could then allow the United States to be considered a transcontinental state. The Aleutian
Islands are sometimes associated with Oceania, owing to their status as remote Pacific islands, and their proximity to
the Pacific Plate. This is extremely rare however, due to their non-tropical biogeography, as well as their inhabitants,
who have historically been related to the <color=#3366CC>Indigenous peoples of the Americas</color>.
St. Lawrence Island in the northern Bering Sea belongs to the US state of <color=#3366CC>Alaska</color> and may be associated with either
continent but is almost always considered part of North America, as with the Rat Islands in the Aleutian chain. At their
nearest points, Alaska and Russia are separated by only 2.5 mi.
Ongoing definition
Geographical Asia is a cultural artifact of European conceptions of the world, beginning with the <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greeks</color>, being
imposed onto other cultures, an imprecise concept causing endemic contention about what it means. Asia does not
exactly correspond to the cultural borders of its various types of constituents.
From the time of Herodotus, a minority of geographers have rejected the three-continent system (Europe, Africa, Asia)
on the grounds that there is no substantial physical separation between them. For example, Sir Barry Cunliffe, the
emeritus professor of European archeology at Oxford, argues that Europe has been geographically and culturally
merely "the western excrescence of the continent of Asia".
Geographically, Asia is the major eastern constituent of the continent of <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color> with Europe being a northwestern
<color=#3366CC>peninsula</color> of the landmass. Asia, Europe and Africa make up a single continuous landmass—<color=#3366CC>Afro-Eurasia</color>—and share
a common <color=#3366CC>continental shelf</color>. Almost all of Europe and a major part of Asia sit atop the <color=#3366CC>Eurasian Plate</color>, adjoined on the
south by the <color=#3366CC>Arabian</color> and Indian Plate and with the easternmost part of Siberia (east of the <color=#3366CC>Chersky Range</color>) on the
<color=#3366CC>North American Plate</color>.
History
Prehistory
About 1.8 million years ago, <color=#3366CC>Homo erectus</color> left the African continent. This species is believed to have lived in East and
Southeast Asia from 1.8 million to 110,000 years ago.
Researchers believe that the modern human, or <color=#3366CC>Homo sapiens</color>, migrated about 60,000 years ago to <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color> along
the Indian Ocean. Modern humans <color=#3366CC>interbred</color> with an <color=#3366CC>archaic human</color> species called <color=#3366CC>Denisovans</color> in Southeast Asia.
Before the arrival of modern humans, <color=#3366CC>Flores</color> was occupied by <color=#3366CC>Homo floresiensis</color>, a small archaic human.
Ancestors of East Eurasians split from Ancient West Eurasians about 46,000 years ago, migrating out of the hub in the
<color=#3366CC>Iranian Plateau</color>. Evidence from full genomic studies suggests that the first people in the Americas diverged from
Ancient East Asians about 36,000 years ago and expanded northwards into Siberia, where they encountered and
interacted with a different Paleolithic Siberian population (known as Ancient North Eurasians), giving rise to both
Paleosiberian peoples and Ancient Native Americans.
Modern South Asians are descendants of a combination of Western Eurasian ancestries (notably Neolithic Iranian and
Western Steppe Herder components) with a proposed indigenous East Eurasian component (termed Ancient Ancestral
South Indians) closest to the non–West Eurasian part extracted from South Asian samples; distantly related to the
Andamanese peoples, East Asians and <color=#3366CC>Aboriginal Australians</color>.
Ancient era
The history of Asia can be seen as the distinct histories of several peripheral coastal regions: <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>West Asia</color>. The coastal periphery was home to some of the world's earliest known
civilisations, each of them developing around fertile river valleys. The civilisations in <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Indus Valley</color> and
the <color=#3366CC>Yellow River</color> shared many similarities. These civilisations may well have exchanged technologies and ideas such
as <color=#3366CC>mathematics</color> and the <color=#3366CC>wheel</color>. Other innovations, such as writing, seem to have been developed individually in each
area. Cities, states and empires developed in these lowlands.
The central steppe region had long been inhabited by horse-mounted nomads who could reach all areas of Asia from
the <color=#3366CC>steppes</color>. The earliest postulated <color=#3366CC>expansion</color> out of the steppe is that of the <color=#3366CC>Indo-Europeans</color>, who spread their
languages into West Asia, South Asia, and the borders of China, where the <color=#3366CC>Tocharians</color> resided. The northernmost part
of Asia, including much of <color=#3366CC>Siberia</color>, was largely inaccessible to the steppe nomads, owing to the dense forests, climate
and <color=#3366CC>tundra</color>. These areas remained very sparsely populated.
The center and the peripheries were mostly kept separated by mountains and deserts. The <color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color> and <color=#3366CC>Himalaya</color>
mountains and the <color=#3366CC>Karakum</color> and <color=#3366CC>Gobi</color> deserts formed barriers that the steppe horsemen could cross only with difficulty.
While the urban city dwellers were more advanced technologically and socially, in many cases they could do little in a
military aspect to defend against the mounted hordes of the steppe. However, the lowlands did not have enough open
grasslands to support a large equestrian force; for this and other reasons, the nomads who conquered states in China,
India, and the Middle East often found themselves adapting to the local, more affluent societies.
Medieval era
The Islamic <color=#3366CC>Caliphate</color>'s defeats of the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine</color> and Persian empires led to West Asia and southern parts of <color=#3366CC>Central</color>
<color=#3366CC>Asia</color> and western parts of South Asia under its control during <color=#3366CC>its conquests</color> of the 7th century; Islam also spread over
centuries to the southern regions of India and Southeast Asia through trade along the <color=#3366CC>Maritime Silk Road</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Mongol</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> conquered a large part of Asia in the 13th century, an area extending from China to Europe. Before the Mongol
invasion, <color=#3366CC>Song dynasty</color> reportedly had approximately 120 million citizens; the 1300 census which followed the invasion
reported roughly 60 million people.
The <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color>, one of the most devastating <color=#3366CC>pandemics</color> in human history, is thought to have originated in the arid
plains of central Asia, where it then travelled along the <color=#3366CC>Silk Road</color>.
Modern era
European involvement in Asia became more significant from the <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color> onward, with Iberian-sponsored
sailors such as <color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus</color> and <color=#3366CC>Vasco da Gama</color> paving the way for new routes from Atlantic Europe to
Pacific Asia and the Indian Ocean respectively in the late 15th century. The <color=#3366CC>Russian Empire</color> also began to expand into
northwestern Asia from the 17th century, and would eventually take control of all of Siberia and most of Central Asia by
the end of the 19th century.
Among non-European empires, the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color> controlled Anatolia, most of the Middle East, North Africa and the
Balkans from the mid 16th century onward, while in the 17th century, the <color=#3366CC>Manchu</color> conquered China and established the
<color=#3366CC>Qing dynasty</color>. The Islamic <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color> (preceded by the <color=#3366CC>Delhi Sultanate</color> of the 13th to early 16th century) and the
Hindu <color=#3366CC>Maratha Empire</color> controlled much of India in the 16th and 18th centuries respectively.
<color=#3366CC>Western imperialism in Asia</color> from the 18th to 20th centuries coincided with the <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color> in the West and the
dethroning of India and China as the world's foremost economies. The <color=#3366CC>British Empire</color> first became dominant in South
Asia, with most of the region being conquered by British traders in the late 18th and early 19th centuries before falling
under <color=#3366CC>direct British rule</color> after a failed <color=#3366CC>1857 revolt</color>; the 1869 completion of the <color=#3366CC>Suez Canal</color>, which increased British
access to India, went on to <color=#3366CC>further European influence</color> over Africa and Asia. Around this time, Western powers started
to dominate China in what later became known as the century of humiliation, with the British-supported opium trade
and later Opium Wars resulting in China being forced into an unprecedented situation of importing more than it
exported.
Foreign domination of China was furthered by the Japanese colonial empire, which controlled some of East Asia and
briefly much of Southeast Asia (which had earlier been taken over by the British, Dutch and French in the late 19th
century), <color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color> and the Pacific islands; Japan's domination was enabled by its rapid rise that had taken place
during the <color=#3366CC>Meiji era</color> of the late 19th century, in which it applied industrial knowledge learned from the West and thus
overtook the rest of Asia. One significant influence on Japan had been the United States, which had begun projecting
influence across the Pacific after its early-to-mid-19th century westward expansion. The breakup of the Ottoman
Empire in the early 20th century led to the Middle East also being <color=#3366CC>contested and partitioned</color> by the British and French.
Contemporary era
With the end of <color=#3366CC>World War II</color> in 1945 and the wartime ruination of Europe and imperial Japan, many countries in Asia
were able to rapidly <color=#3366CC>free themselves</color> of colonial rule. The <color=#3366CC>independence of India</color> came along with the <color=#3366CC>carving out</color> of a
separate nation for the majority of South Asian Muslims, which in 1971 <color=#3366CC>further split</color> into Pakistan and <color=#3366CC>Bangladesh</color>; The
Cold War in Asia strained relations between India and Pakistan and affected Asia more generally. The end of the Cold
War and the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> by 1991 saw the independence of the five modern Central Asian countries.
Some Arab countries took economic advantage of massive oil deposits that were discovered in their territory, becoming
globally influential, though stability in the Middle East has been affected since 1948 by the <color=#3366CC>Arab–Israeli conflict</color> and
American-led interventions. East Asian nations (along with Singapore in Southeast Asia) became economically
prosperous with high-growth "tiger economies"; China, having undergone the <color=#3366CC>reform and opening up</color> under <color=#3366CC>Deng</color>
<color=#3366CC>Xiaoping</color>, regained its place among the top two economies of the world by the 21st century. India has also grown
significantly because of economic liberalisation that started in the 1990s, with extreme poverty now below 20%; India
and China's rise has coincided with growing tensions between the two, with the Indo-Pacific now an actively contested
area between China and counterbalancing forces.
Geography
Asia is the largest continent on Earth. It covers 9% of the Earth's total surface area (or 30% of its land area), and has
the longest coastline, at 62800 km. Asia is generally defined as comprising the eastern four-fifths of Eurasia. It is
located to the east of the <color=#3366CC>Suez Canal</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Ural Mountains</color>, and south of the <color=#3366CC>Caucasus Mountains</color> (or the
Kuma–Manych Depression) and the <color=#3366CC>Caspian</color> and <color=#3366CC>Black Seas</color>. It is bounded on the east by the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean</color>, on the
south by the Indian Ocean and on the north by the Arctic Ocean. Asia is subdivided into 49 countries, five of them

(<color=#3366CC>Georgia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Azerbaijan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Russia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kazakhstan</color> and <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color>) are transcontinental countries lying partly in Europe.
The <color=#3366CC>Yangtze</color> in China is the longest river in the continent. The Himalayas between Nepal and China is the tallest
mountain range in the world. <color=#3366CC>Tropical rainforests</color> stretch across much of southern Asia and coniferous and deciduous
forests lie farther north. Between 1990 and 2000 the area of primary forest in Asia decreased by 1.06 million hectares
per year, between 2000 and 2015 it decreased by 280 000 ha per year.
Main regions
There are various approaches to the regional division of Asia. The following subdivision into regions is used, among
others, by the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD). This division of Asia into regions by the United Nations is
done solely for statistical reasons and does not imply any assumption about political or other affiliations of countries
and territories.
• <color=#3366CC>North Asia</color> (<color=#3366CC>Siberia</color>)
• <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>
• <color=#3366CC>West Asia</color> (the <color=#3366CC>Middle East</color> or <color=#3366CC>Near East</color> and part of the <color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color>)
• <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color> (<color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>)
• <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color> (<color=#3366CC>Far East</color>)
• <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color> (East Indies and <color=#3366CC>Indochina</color>)
Climate
Asia has extremely diverse climate features. Climates range from <color=#3366CC>Arctic</color> and <color=#3366CC>subarctic</color> in Siberia to tropical in southern
India and Southeast Asia. It is moist across southeast sections, and dry across much of the interior. Some of the
largest daily temperature ranges on Earth occur in western sections of Asia. The <color=#3366CC>monsoon</color> circulation dominates across
southern and eastern sections, due to the presence of the Himalayas forcing the formation of a thermal low which
draws in moisture during the summer. Southwestern sections of the continent are hot. Siberia is one of the coldest
places in the <color=#3366CC>Northern Hemisphere</color>, and can act as a source of arctic air masses for North America. The most active
place on Earth for <color=#3366CC>tropical cyclone</color> activity lies northeast of the <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color> and south of Japan.

Politics

indices.

Economy
Asia is both the largest continental economy in the world by both GDP nominal and <color=#3366CC>PPP</color> values and the world's fastest
growing economic region. As of 2026, <color=#3366CC>China</color> is by far the largest economy on the continent. It is followed by India,
Japan, South Korea, Turkey, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and Taiwan, which are all ranked among the top 20 largest
economies by both nominal GDP and PPP values. Based on Global Office Locations 2011, Asia dominated global

office locations with 4 of the top 5 being in Asia: <color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color>, <color=#3366CC>Singapore</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tokyo</color> and <color=#3366CC>Seoul</color>. Around 68% of international
firms have an office in Hong Kong.
In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the economy of China had an average annual growth rate of more than 8%.
According to economic historian Angus Maddison, India had the world's largest economy for much of the past three
millennia prior to the 19th century, accounting for 25% of the world's industrial output. China was the largest and most
advanced economy on Earth for much of recorded history and shared the mantle with India. For several decades in the
late twentieth century, Japan was the largest economy in Asia and second-largest in the world, after surpassing the
<color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> (measured in net material product) in 1990 and Germany in 1968. This ended in 2010, when China
overtook Japan to become the world's second largest economy. In 2025, India overtook Japan in terms of nominal GDP
to become the world's 4th largest and Asia's 2nd largest economy.
In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Japan's GDP by currency exchange rates was almost as large as that of the rest of
Asia combined. In 1995, Japan's economy nearly equaled that of the US as the largest economy in the world for a day,
after the Japanese currency reached a record high of 79 <color=#3366CC>yen</color>/US$. Economic growth in Asia since <color=#3366CC>World War II</color> to the
1990s had been concentrated in Japan as well as South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Singapore, known as the
<color=#3366CC>Four Asian Tigers</color>, which are now all considered developed economies, having among the highest GDP per capita in
Asia.
Asia is the largest continent in the world by a considerable margin, and it is rich in natural resources, such as

<color=#3366CC>petroleum</color>, <color=#3366CC>forests</color>, <color=#3366CC>fish</color>, <color=#3366CC>water</color>, <color=#3366CC>rice</color>, <color=#3366CC>copper</color> and <color=#3366CC>silver</color>. Manufacturing in Asia has traditionally been strongest in East
and Southeast Asia, particularly in China, <color=#3366CC>Taiwan</color>, South Korea, Japan, India, the Philippines, and Singapore. Japan
and South Korea continue to dominate in the area of <color=#3366CC>multinational corporations</color>, though increasingly China and India
are making significant inroads. Many companies from Europe, North America, South Korea, and Japan have operations
in Asia's developing countries to take advantage of its abundant supply of cheap labour and relatively developed
infrastructure.
According to Citigroup in 2011, 9 of 11 Global Growth Generator countries came from Asia driven by population and
income growth. They are Bangladesh, China, India, Indonesia, Iraq, Mongolia, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, and Vietnam.
Asia has three main financial centers: Hong Kong, Tokyo, and Singapore. Call centers and business process
outsourcing firms (BPOs) are becoming major employers in India and the Philippines due to the availability of a large
pool of highly skilled, English-speaking workers. The increased use of outsourcing has assisted the rise of India and the
China as financial centers. Due to its large and extremely competitive information technology industry, India has
become a major hub for outsourcing.
Trade between Asian countries and countries on other continents is largely carried out via sea routes. The main route
leads from the Chinese coast south via Hanoi to Jakarta, Singapore, and Kuala Lumpur, through the <color=#3366CC>Strait of Malacca</color>
via <color=#3366CC>Colombo</color> to the southern tip of India, then via Malé to <color=#3366CC>Mombasa</color> in East Africa (see also Indo-Pacific), from there to
<color=#3366CC>Djibouti</color>, then through the Red Sea and the <color=#3366CC>Suez Canal</color> into the Mediterranean (see also: Indo-Mediterranean), then via
Haifa, Istanbul, and <color=#3366CC>Athens</color> to the northern Italian hub of <color=#3366CC>Trieste</color>, with its rail connections to Central and Eastern
Europe, or further to <color=#3366CC>Barcelona</color> and around Spain and France to northern European ports. A far smaller part of the
goods traffic runs via South Africa to Europe. A particularly significant part of Asian goods traffic is carried out on the
Pacific Rim, toward <color=#3366CC>Los Angeles</color> and <color=#3366CC>Long Beach</color>. The melting of the Arctic is also paving the way for new shipping
routes from Northeast Asia to Europe and North America. The land route to Europe is also the subject of construction
projects, comparatively smaller in scope. Intra-Asian trade, including sea trade, is growing rapidly.
In 2010, Asia had 3.3 million millionaires (people with net worth over US$1 million excluding their homes), slightly
below North America's 3.4 million. In 2011, Asia topped Europe in the number of millionaires. Citigroup in The Wealth
Report 2012 stated that the total wealth of people in Asia with over $100 million in assets exceeded that of their North
American counterparts for the first time, as the world's "economic center of gravity" continued moving east. At the end
of 2011, there were 18,000 people in Asia, mainly in Southeast Asia, China, and Japan, with at least $100 million in
disposable assets, compared to North America with 17,000 and Western Europe with 14,000.
Energy
Asia's electricity demand has quadrupled since 2000 (rising from 4,199 TWh to over 16,000 TWh in 2024). This growth,
driven largely by China and increasingly by India, Indonesia, and Viet Nam, makes Asia the fastest-growing region for
electricity demand globally, at about 5% per year. The region now accounts for about 36% of global primary energy
consumption, a share projected to approach 50% by 2050.: 1468 <color=#3366CC>Fossil fuels</color> remain central in Asia: 66% of its energy
is generated from fossil fuels, and Asia makes up 83% of the world's coal generation. However, coal is slowly being
phased out and <color=#3366CC>natural gas</color> is displacing oil and oil products in various sectors, supported by policies and regulations.
Natural gas demand in emerging market and developing economies in Asia expanded by around 6% in 2024,
accounting for nearly 40% of incremental global gas demand. By 2040, Asia is expected to account for the majority of
global coal use and over a quarter of natural gas consumption.: 1468
At the same time, Asia is the global leader in <color=#3366CC>renewable energy</color> expansion. It is currently the only region on track to
meet the goal of tripling renewable capacity by 2030, largely due to China, the leading nation in renewable energy
generation. China's wind and solar capacity has surged in recent years, together overtaking that of coal, while in 2024
India become the world's third largest generator of electricity from wind and solar. Nearly half of the world's new
renewable energy capacity is built in Asia.: 1470
Tourism
In 2013, with regional tourism growing and dominated by Chinese visitors, <color=#3366CC>MasterCard</color> released the Global Destination
Cities Index report, in which 10 of 20 cities are Asian and Pacific cities. This was also the first time an Asian city
(<color=#3366CC>Bangkok</color>) was in the number one spot, with 15.98 million international visitors.
Demographics
East Asia had by far the strongest overall <color=#3366CC>Human Development Index</color> (HDI) improvement of any region in the world,
nearly doubling average HDI attainment over the past 40 years, according to the report's analysis of health, education
and income data. China, the second highest achiever in the world in terms of HDI improvement since 1970, is the only
country on the "Top 10 Movers" list due to income rather than health or education achievements. Its per capita income
increased a stunning 21-fold over the last four decades, also lifting hundreds of millions out of income poverty. Yet it
was not among the region's top performers in improving school enrollment and life expectancy. <color=#3366CC>Nepal</color>, a South Asian
country, emerges as one of the world's fastest movers since 1970 mainly due to health and education achievements.
Its present <color=#3366CC>life expectancy</color> is 25 years longer than in the 1970s. More than four of every five children of school age in
Nepal now attend primary school, compared to just one in five 40 years ago. Hong Kong ranked highest among the
countries grouped on the HDI (number 7 in the world, which is in the "very high human development" category),
followed by Singapore (9), Japan (19) and South Korea (22). <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color> (155) ranked lowest amongst Asian countries
out of the 169 countries assessed.
Languages
Asia is home to several <color=#3366CC>language families</color> and many <color=#3366CC>language isolates</color>. Most Asian countries have more than one
language that is natively spoken. For instance, according to Ethnologue, more than 700 languages are spoken in
Indonesia, more than 400 languages spoken in India, and more than 100 are spoken in the Philippines. China has
many languages and dialects in different provinces.
Religions
Many of the world's major religions have their origins in Asia, including the five most practiced in the world (excluding
<color=#3366CC>irreligion</color>), which are Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Chinese folk religion (classified as Confucianism and Taoism), and
Buddhism. Asian mythology is complex and diverse. The story of the <color=#3366CC>Great Flood</color> for example, as presented to <color=#3366CC>Jews</color> in
the <color=#3366CC>Hebrew Bible (Tanakh)</color> in the narrative of <color=#3366CC>Noah</color>—later translated from <color=#3366CC>Hebrew</color> to <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> and included in

<color=#3366CC>Christanity’s</color> <color=#3366CC>Old Testament</color>, and to Muslims in the <color=#3366CC>Quran</color>—is earliest found in <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamian mythology</color>, in the <color=#3366CC>Enûma</color>

<color=#3366CC>Eliš</color> and <color=#3366CC>Epic of Gilgamesh</color>. <color=#3366CC>Hindu mythology</color> similarly tells about an <color=#3366CC>avatar</color> of <color=#3366CC>Vishnu</color> in the form of a fish who warned
Manu of a terrible flood. Ancient <color=#3366CC>Chinese mythology</color> also tells of a <color=#3366CC>Great Flood</color> spanning generations, one that required
the combined efforts of emperors and divinities to control.
Abrahamic

The <color=#3366CC>Abrahamic religions</color> including <color=#3366CC>Judaism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>, <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, <color=#3366CC>Druze faith</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Baháí Faith</color> originated in West Asia.
<color=#3366CC>Judaism</color>, the oldest of the Abrahamic faiths, is practiced primarily in <color=#3366CC>Israel</color>, the indigenous homeland and historical
birthplace of the <color=#3366CC>Hebrew nation</color>: which today consists both of those Jews who remained in the Middle East and those
who returned from the diaspora in Europe, North America, <color=#3366CC>Ethiopia</color>, India, and other regions, though various Israelite
diaspora communities still exist worldwide. Jews are the predominant ethnic group in Israel (75.6%) numbering at about
6.1 million. Levels of Jewish religious observance vary within the Jewish State. Outside of Israel, there are small
ancient Jewish communities in <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color> (17,400), <color=#3366CC>Azerbaijan</color> (9,100), Iran (8,756), India (5,000) and <color=#3366CC>Uzbekistan</color> (4,000),
among many other places. As of 2016, there are am estimated 14.4–17.5 million (2016, est.) Jews alive in the world
today, making them one of the smallest Asian minorities, at roughly 0.3–0.4& of the total population of the continent.
<color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> is a widespread religion in Asia, with more than 286 million adherents in 2010 according to Pew Research
Center, and nearly 364 million according to <color=#3366CC>Britannica</color> Book of the Year 2014. Christians constitute around 12.6% of the
total population of Asia. In the Philippines and <color=#3366CC>Timor-Leste</color>, <color=#3366CC>Catholicism</color> is the predominant religion; it was introduced
by the Spaniards and the Portuguese, respectively. In <color=#3366CC>Armenia</color> and Georgia, <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodoxy</color> is the predominant
religion. In the Middle East, such as in the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>, <color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color> and Fars, Syriac Christianity (<color=#3366CC>Church of the East</color>) and
<color=#3366CC>Oriental Orthodoxy</color> are prevalent minority denominations, which are both <color=#3366CC>Eastern Christian</color> sects mainly adhered to
Assyrian people or Syriac Christians. Vibrant indigenous minorities in <color=#3366CC>West Asia</color> are adhering to the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Catholic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Churches</color> and Eastern Orthodoxy. Saint Thomas Christians in India trace their origins to the evangelistic activity of
<color=#3366CC>Thomas the Apostle</color> in the 1st century. Significant Christian communities also found in <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color> and <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, which originated in the <color=#3366CC>Hejaz</color> located in modern-day Saudi Arabia, is the second largest and most widely-spread
religion in Asia with at least 1 billion Muslims constituting around 23.8% of the total population of Asia. With 12.7% of
the world Muslim population, the country currently with the largest Muslim population in the world is Indonesia, followed
by Pakistan (11.5%), India (10%), Bangladesh, Iran and Turkey. <color=#3366CC>Mecca</color>, <color=#3366CC>Medina</color> and Jerusalem are the three holiest
cities for Islam in all the world. The <color=#3366CC>Hajj</color> and Umrah attract large numbers of Muslim devotees from all over the world to
Mecca and Medina. Iran is the largest <color=#3366CC>Shia</color> country.
The <color=#3366CC>Druze</color> originated in West Asia, is a monotheistic religion based on the teachings of figures like Hamza ibn Ali and

<color=#3366CC>al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah</color>, and Greek <color=#3366CC>philosophers</color> such as <color=#3366CC>Plato</color> and <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>. The number of Druze people worldwide is
around one million. Around 45–50% live in <color=#3366CC>Syria</color>, 35% to 40% live in <color=#3366CC>Lebanon</color>, and less than 10% live in <color=#3366CC>Israel</color>.
Recently there has been a growing Druze diaspora.
The <color=#3366CC>Baháí Faith</color> originated in Asia, in Iran (Persia), and spread from there to the Ottoman Empire, Central Asia, India,
and Burma during the lifetime of <color=#3366CC>Bahá'u'lláh</color>. Since the middle of the 20th century, growth has particularly occurred in
other Asian countries, because Baháí activities in many Muslim countries has been severely suppressed by authorities.
Lotus Temple is a big Baháí temple in India.
Indian and East Asian religions
Almost all Asian religions have philosophical character and Asian philosophical traditions cover a large spectrum of
philosophical thoughts and writings. <color=#3366CC>Indian philosophy</color> includes <color=#3366CC>Hindu philosophy</color> and <color=#3366CC>Buddhist philosophy</color>. They
include elements of nonmaterial pursuits, whereas another school of thought from India, <color=#3366CC>Cārvāka</color>, preached the

enjoyment of the material world. The religions of <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jainism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sikhism</color> originated in India, South
Asia. In East Asia, particularly in China and Japan, <color=#3366CC>Confucianism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Taoism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Zen</color> Buddhism took shape.
As of 2012, Hinduism has around 1.1 billion adherents. The faith represents around 25% of Asia's population and is the
largest religion in Asia. However, it is mostly concentrated in South Asia. Over 80% of the populations of both India and
Nepal adhere to Hinduism, alongside significant communities in Bangladesh, Pakistan, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and <color=#3366CC>Bali</color>,
Indonesia. Many overseas Indians in countries such as Burma, Singapore and Malaysia also adhere to Hinduism.
Buddhism has a great following in <color=#3366CC>Mainland Southeast Asia</color> and East Asia. Buddhism is the religion of the majority of

the populations of Cambodia (96%), <color=#3366CC>Thailand</color> (95%), <color=#3366CC>Burma</color> (80–89%), Japan (36–96%), <color=#3366CC>Bhutan</color> (75–84%), <color=#3366CC>Sri Lanka</color>

(70%), <color=#3366CC>Laos</color> (60–67%) and <color=#3366CC>Mongolia</color> (53–93%). <color=#3366CC>Taiwan</color> (35–93%), South Korea (23–50%), <color=#3366CC>Malaysia</color> (19–21%), <color=#3366CC>Nepal</color>
(9–11%), <color=#3366CC>Vietnam</color> (10–75%), China (20–50%), <color=#3366CC>Singapore</color> (31%), <color=#3366CC>North Korea</color> (2–14%), and small communities in India
and Bangladesh. The Communist-governed countries of China, Vietnam and North Korea are officially atheist, thus the
number of Buddhists and other religious adherents may be under-reported.
<color=#3366CC>Jainism</color> is found mainly in India and in overseas Indian communities such as the United States and Malaysia. <color=#3366CC>Sikhism</color>
is found in Northern India and amongst overseas Indian communities in other parts of Asia, especially Southeast Asia.
<color=#3366CC>Confucianism</color> is found predominantly in mainland China, South Korea, Taiwan and in overseas Chinese populations.
<color=#3366CC>Taoism</color> is found mainly in mainland China, Taiwan, Malaysia and Singapore. In many Chinese communities, Taoism is
easily syncretised with <color=#3366CC>Mahayana Buddhism</color>, thus exact religious statistics are difficult to obtain and may be
understated or overstated.
Culture
The <color=#3366CC>culture of Asia</color> is a diverse blend of customs and traditions that have been practiced by the various ethnic groups
of the continent for centuries. The continent is divided into six geographic sub-regions: <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>North</color>
<color=#3366CC>Asia</color>, South Asia, <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>West Asia</color>. These regions are defined by their cultural similarities, including
common religions, languages, and ethnicities. West Asia, also known as Southwest Asia or the <color=#3366CC>Middle East</color>, has

cultural roots in the ancient civilisations of the <color=#3366CC>Fertile Crescent</color> and <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color>, which gave rise to the <color=#3366CC>Persian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Arab</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Ottoman</color> empires, as well as the Abrahamic religions of Judaism, Christianity and Islam. These civilisations, which are
located in the Hilly flanks, are among the oldest in the world, with evidence of farming dating back to around 9000 BCE.
Despite the challenges posed by the vast size of the continent and the presence of natural barriers such as deserts and
mountain ranges, trade and commerce have helped to create a Pan-Asian culture that is shared across the region.
Nobel laureates
<color=#3366CC>Rabindranath Tagore</color>, a <color=#3366CC>Bengali</color> dramatist and author from Santiniketan (now in <color=#3366CC>West Bengal</color>, India), won the Nobel
Prize in Literature in 1913, becoming the first Asian Nobel laureate. The prize was awarded for Tagore's prose works
and poetry, which had a significant additional impact on national literatures throughout the Western world. Tagore also
authored both the Indian and Bangladeshi national anthems.
Other Asian writers who won Nobel Prize for literature include <color=#3366CC>Yasunari Kawabata</color> (Japan, 1968), <color=#3366CC>Kenzaburō Ōe</color>

(Japan, 1994), <color=#3366CC>Gao Xingjian</color> (China, 2000), <color=#3366CC>Orhan Pamuk</color> (Turkey, 2006), <color=#3366CC>Mo Yan</color> (China, 2012), and <color=#3366CC>Han Kang</color> (South
Korea, 2024). Some may consider the American writer, <color=#3366CC>Pearl S. Buck</color>, an honorary Asian Nobel laureate, having spent
considerable time in China as the daughter of missionaries, and based many of her novels, namely <color=#3366CC>The Good Earth</color>
(1931) and The Mother (1933), as well as the biographies of her parents for their time in China, The Exile and Fighting
Angel, all of which earned her the Literature prize in 1938.
<color=#3366CC>Mother Teresa</color> of India and <color=#3366CC>Shirin Ebadi</color> of Iran were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for their significant and
pioneering efforts for <color=#3366CC>democracy</color> and human rights, especially for the rights of women and children. Ebadi is the first
Iranian and the first Muslim woman to receive the prize. Another Nobel Peace Prize winner is <color=#3366CC>Aung San Suu Kyi</color> from
<color=#3366CC>Burma</color> for her peaceful and non-violent struggle under a military dictatorship in Burma. She is a nonviolent
pro-democracy activist and leader of the National League for Democracy in Burma (Myanmar) and a noted prisoner of
conscience. She is a Buddhist and was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991. Chinese dissident <color=#3366CC>Liu Xiaobo</color> was
awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for "his long and non-violent struggle for fundamental human rights in China" on 8
October 2010. He is the first Chinese citizen to be awarded a Nobel Prize of any kind while residing in China. In 2014,
<color=#3366CC>Kailash Satyarthi</color> from India and <color=#3366CC>Malala Yousafzai</color> from Pakistan were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize "for their
struggle against the suppression of children and young people and for the right of all children to education".
<color=#3366CC>C.V. Raman</color> is the first Asian to get a Nobel prize in Sciences. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics "for his work on the
scattering of light and for the discovery of the effect named after him".
Japan has won the most Nobel Prizes of any Asian nation with 24 followed by India which has won 13.
<color=#3366CC>Amartya Sen</color> (b. 1933) is an Indian economist who was awarded the 1998 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
for his contributions to welfare economics and <color=#3366CC>social choice theory</color>, and for his interest in the problems of society's
poorest members.
Other Asian Nobel Prize winners include <color=#3366CC>Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar</color>, <color=#3366CC>Abdus Salam</color>, <color=#3366CC>Robert Aumann</color>, <color=#3366CC>Menachem</color>

<color=#3366CC>Begin</color>, Aaron Ciechanover, Avram Hershko, <color=#3366CC>Daniel Kahneman</color>, <color=#3366CC>Shimon Peres</color>, <color=#3366CC>Yitzhak Rabin</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ada Yonath</color>, <color=#3366CC>Yasser</color>

<color=#3366CC>Arafat</color>, <color=#3366CC>José Ramos-Horta</color> and Bishop <color=#3366CC>Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo</color> of <color=#3366CC>Timor-Leste</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kim Dae-jung</color>, and 13 Japanese
scientists. Most of the said awardees are from Japan and <color=#3366CC>Israel</color> except for Chandrasekhar and Raman (India), Abdus
Salam (Pakistan), Arafat (Palestinian Territories), Kim (South Korea), and Horta and Belo (Timor-Leste).
In 2006, the Bangladeshi <color=#3366CC>Muhammad Yunus</color> of was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for the establishment of <color=#3366CC>Grameen</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bank</color>, a community development bank that lends money to poor people, especially women. He is known for the
concept of micro credit which, allows poor and destitute people to borrow money. The borrowers pay back money
within the specified period and defaulting is very low. Yunus also became the leader of an interim government after the
2024 Bangladesh quota reform movement. The <color=#3366CC>Dalai Lama</color> received the Nobel Peace Prize, in <color=#3366CC>Oslo</color>, Norway in 1989.
